# maynard-mosaic-theory-2010
- **URL:** https://media.cadc.uscourts.gov/opinions/docs/2010/08/08-3030-1259298.pdf (D.C. Circuit official slip opinion; also https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-caDC-08-03030/pdf/USCOURTS-caDC-08-03030-0.pdf) and Kerr: https://repository.law.umich.edu/mlr/vol111/iss3/1/ · **Accessed:** 2026-08-25 · **For:** v1→v2 response round, aggregation/mosaic doctrine anchor
- **What it establishes:** *United States v. Maynard*, 615 F.3d 544 (D.C. Cir. 2010) (Ginsburg, D.H., J.) held that warrantless GPS tracking of Antoine Jones's Jeep "24 hours a day for four weeks" (elsewhere "28 days") was a Fourth Amendment search, because the *whole* of one's movements over a month is not exposed to the public even though each individual movement is — the whole reveals more than the sum of its parts. This is the aggregation argument in judicial form; Orin Kerr, "The Mosaic Theory of the Fourth Amendment," 111 Mich. L. Rev. 311 (2012), names and criticizes it. Lineage: Maynard → *United States v. Jones*, 565 U.S. 400 (2012) (affirmed sub nom. on trespass grounds; five Justices' concurrences — Sotomayor; Alito joined by Ginsburg, Breyer, Kagan — endorse aggregation reasoning) → *Carpenter v. United States*, 138 S. Ct. 2206 (2018) (extends the logic to historical cell-site location records; "provides an intimate window into a person's life" — search-level; verify before print quotation).
- **Key passages:** (verbatim from the slip opinion PDF; PDF text-layer spacing artifacts normalized only within words, e.g. "one 's"→"one's")
  - Two-part exposure argument (slip op. 22): "Two considerations persuade us the information the police discovered in this case—the totality of Jones's movements over the course of a month—was not exposed to the public: First, unlike one's movements during a single journey, the whole of one's movements over the course of a month is not actually exposed to the public because the likelihood anyone will observe all those movements is effectively nil. Second, the whole of one's movements is not exposed constructively even though each individual movement is exposed, because that whole reveals more—sometimes a great deal more—than does the sum of its parts."
  - Whole vs. parts, difference in kind (slip op. 28–29): "The whole of one's movements over the course of a month is not constructively exposed to the public because, like a rap sheet, that whole reveals far more than the individual movements it comprises. The difference is not one of degree but of kind, for no single journey reveals the habits and patterns that mark the distinction between a day in the life and a way of life, nor the departure from a routine that, like the dog that did not bark in the Sherlock Holmes story, may reveal even more."
  - The court itself invokes the "mosaic" label (slip op. 29): "As with the 'mosaic theory' often invoked by the Government in cases involving national security information, 'What may seem trivial to the uninformed, may appear of great moment to one who has a broad view of the scene.' CIA v. Sims, 471 U.S. 159, 178 (1985)…"
  - What prolonged surveillance reveals (slip op. 29): "Prolonged surveillance reveals types of information not revealed by short-term surveillance, such as what a person does repeatedly, what he does not do, and what he does ensemble. These types of information can each reveal more about a person than does any individual trip viewed in isolation. Repeated visits to a church, a gym, a bar, or a bookie tell a story not told by any single visit, as does one's not visiting any of these places over the course of a month. The sequence of a person's movements can reveal still more; a single trip to a gynecologist's office tells little about a woman, but that trip followed a few weeks later by a visit to a baby supply store tells a different story."
  - Deduction passage (slip op. 30): "A person who knows all of another's travels can deduce whether he is a weekly church goer, a heavy drinker, a regular at the gym, an unfaithful husband, an outpatient receiving medical treatment, an associate of particular individuals or political groups—and not just one such fact about a person, but all such facts."
  - Facts/duration (slip op. 15–16): tracking "his movements 24 hours a day for four weeks with a GPS device they had installed on his Jeep without a valid warrant"; also "track Jones's movements 24 hours a day for 28 days as he moved among scores of places."
  - Holding framing (slip op. 16): "we hold Knotts does not govern this case and the police action was a search because it defeated Jones's reasonable expectation of privacy."
  - NOTE: the often-quoted "familial, political, professional, religious, and sexual associations" line is NOT Maynard's own — it is *People v. Weaver*, 909 N.E.2d 1194, 1199 (N.Y. 2009), quoted by Maynard and later by Sotomayor's *Jones* concurrence (search-level; verify before print quotation).
  - Kerr (111 Mich. L. Rev. 311 (2012)), from the article/abstract: under the mosaic theory courts "evaluate a collective sequence of government activity as an aggregated whole to consider whether the sequence amounts to a search"; "Before Jones, Fourth Amendment decisions had always evaluated each step of an investigation individually"; Kerr concludes "courts should reject the theory and retain the traditional sequential approach to Fourth Amendment analysis." (Fetched via repository page summary — treat these three as near-verbatim but re-check against the PDF before print quotation.)
- **Reliability:** Maynard: primary (official D.C. Circuit slip opinion PDF, quotes checked in context). Kerr: secondary scholarship, and adversarial to the mosaic theory — useful as the theory's namer AND as the steelman critic (he coined the frame while arguing against it; citing him for the definition is citing a critic, which strengthens neutrality).
- **Relevance to this project:** The doctrinal twin of the essay's aggregation claim — that totalizing visibility differs in kind, not degree, from episodic observation; supplies court-tested language for the "whole reveals more than the parts" argument and the bridge from GPS (Maynard/Jones) to cell-site data (Carpenter). Cite as: United States v. Maynard, 615 F.3d 544, 561–63 (D.C. Cir. 2010), aff'd in part sub nom. United States v. Jones, 565 U.S. 400 (2012); Orin S. Kerr, The Mosaic Theory of the Fourth Amendment, 111 Mich. L. Rev. 311 (2012).
